chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, from Khalid ibn Bukayr al-Tawil, who said:

My father called me when death approached him and said: 'O my son, collect the wealth of your young brothers, invest it, take half the profit for yourself, and give them the other half, and there is no guarantee (liability) upon you.'
After my father's death, a mother of a child (his wife) presented me to Ibn Abi Layla and said: 'This one is eating the wealth of my children.'
Ibn Abi Layla said: 'If your father commanded you with what is false (unjust), I would not validate it.'
Then Ibn Abi Layla testified against me: 'If I move (displace) him, I am liable for it.'
After that, I entered upon Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and recounted my story to him, then I said to him: 'What do you think?'
He said: 'As for the statement of Ibn Abi Layla, I cannot refute it; but as for what is between you and Allah, there is no guarantee upon you.'

key_terms.أُمُّ وَلَدٍ: Mother of a child (concubine or wife who bore children)
key_terms.اِبْنُ أَبِي لَيْلَى: A prominent judge (qadi) of the era

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a father instructing his son to manage siblings' wealth with a share of profit and no liability?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Shia juristic distinction between civil liability (*daman*) and spiritual accountability (*mas'uliyya*) in estate management. While the judge Ibn Abi Layla validated the father's instruction as legally binding in court, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarified that the son bears no divine liability for losses, emphasizing that the father's directive was valid even if not strictly 'correct' in all legal nuances. This highlights the Shia principle that a guardian's specific instructions, if not explicitly contrary to Sharia, are respected, with the ultimate judgment resting on the Imam's spiritual insight.
